steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on probability-based prompt selection for large language models. It should explain why prompt choice matters, point out that existing selection methods have never been compared fairly, and introduce our unified evaluation, the new method variants it leads to, and our calibration method.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- LLMs, prompt-based learning, sensitivity to the choice of prompt
- Probability-based prompt selection and the lack of a fair comparison
- Unified evaluation setup; MI-based combinational variants
- Better probability estimates: Calibration By Marginalization (CBM)

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- LLMs and prompts
  - remarkable performance on NLP tasks via prompt-based learning, no additional task-specific training
  - performance fluctuates heavily with choice of prompt
  - many prompt engineering approaches, but prerequisites (training an additional model, using an additional component) bottleneck real application
- Probability-based prompt selection
  - no additional parameter updates or components -> promising, easily applicable
  - selects from a set of prompts the one expected to most help the model predict correctly, based solely on the model's probability distribution
  - but: no comprehensive comparative evaluation; each method has different setup, datasets, evaluation instances, prompt sets, models
- Our unified evaluation
  - carefully designed for fair comparison
  - no single method consistently best across all datasets
  - all existing methods roughly correspond to a sub-term of the Mutual Information (MI) equation
  - propose MI variants combining components of existing methods
  - best combinational variant MI {}_{\textnormal{AGL}}: scaled F1 (F1 / oracle prompt F1) 87.79% -> 94.98% (Figure 1(a))
- Calibration
  - all methods rely on model probability estimates, possibly biased -> need better approximation of output distribution
  - connect existing output probability calibration methods -> Calibration By Marginalization (CBM)
  - best scaled F1 96.85% (MI {}_{\text{A}}^{\text{(PA)}}, Figure 1(a)); 99.44% of oracle prompt F1 under uncalibrated scenario
  - most robust answer selection enhancement across datasets vs existing calibration methods (Figure 1(b))

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performance on many natural language processing tasks by using prompt-based learning, without needing additional task-specific training. However, how well LLMs perform can fluctuate a lot depending on which prompt is chosen. Various prompt engineering approaches have been proposed to deal with this, but many of them have nontrivial prerequisites, like training an additional model and/or using an additional component, and this has been a bottleneck for actually applying them.

Probability-based prompt selection methods, on the other hand, do not need any additional parameter updates or additional components, so they are a promising solution that is easy to apply. These methods try to select, from a set of prompts, the prompt that is expected to be the most effective at helping a language model make correct predictions, and they do this only based on the probability distribution of the model. But even though they are easy to use, there has not been a comprehensive comparative evaluation of the existing probability-based prompt selection methods, because each method was proposed in a different setup and evaluated on different datasets, evaluation instances, sets of prompts, and models.

  - no single method consistently best across all datasets
  - all existing methods roughly correspond to a sub-term of the Mutual Information (MI) equation
  - propose MI variants combining components of existing methods
  - best combinational variant MI {}_{\textnormal{AGL}}: scaled F1 (F1 / oracle prompt F1) 87.79% -> 94.98% (Figure 1(a))
- Calibration
  - all methods rely on model probability estimates, possibly biased -> need better approximation of output distribution
  - connect existing output probability calibration methods -> Calibration By Marginalization (CBM)
  - best scaled F1 96.85% (MI {}_{\text{A}}^{\text{(PA)}}, Figure 1(a)); 99.44% of oracle prompt F1 under uncalibrated scenario
  - most robust answer selection enhancement across datasets vs existing calibration methods (Figure 1(b))

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performance on many natural language processing tasks by using prompt-based learning, without needing additional task-specific training. However, how well LLMs perform can fluctuate a lot depending on which prompt is chosen. Various prompt engineering approaches have been proposed to deal with this, but many of them have nontrivial prerequisites, like training an additional model and/or using an additional component, and this has been a bottleneck for actually applying them.

Probability-based prompt selection methods, on the other hand, do not need any additional parameter updates or additional components, so they are a promising solution that is easy to apply. These methods try to select, from a set of prompts, the prompt that is expected to be the most effective at helping a language model make correct predictions, and they do this only based on the probability distribution of the model. But even though they are easy to use, there has not been a comprehensive comparative evaluation of the existing probability-based prompt selection methods, because each method was proposed in a different setup and evaluated on different datasets, evaluation instances, sets of prompts, and models.

In this paper, we first design a unified evaluation setup so that different prompt selection methods can be compared fairly. The unified evaluation shows that no single method consistently does better than the other methods across all datasets. It also shows that all existing probability-based prompt selection methods roughly correspond to a sub-term of the equation of Mutual Information (MI). We use this finding to propose several variants of MI that combine the components of existing methods in different ways. The best combinational variant, MI {}_{\textnormal{AGL}}, increases the scaled F1 from 87.79% to 94.98% (MI {}_{\textnormal{AGL}} of Figure 1(a)). The scaled F1 is the F1 divided by the F1 of the oracle prompt, and it shows how effective the prompt selection method is.

We also find that we need a better approximation of the output probability distribution of the LLM, since all probability-based prompt selection methods rely on probabilistic estimates from the model, and these might be biased. So, by drawing a connection between existing model output probability calibration methods, we propose an enhanced calibration method, Calibration By Marginalization (CBM). When CBM is applied to calibrate the output probability of LLMs, it significantly improves the prompt selection performance of several methods. It increases the best scaled F1 to 96.85% (MI {}_{\text{A}}^{\text{(PA)}} of Figure 1(a)), which is 99.44% of the oracle prompt F1 under the uncalibrated scenario. CBM also shows the most robust answer selection enhancement across multiple datasets when compared to the existing calibration methods (Figure 1(b)).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance in solving various natural language processing tasks through prompt-based learning, without requiring additional task-specific training [1,2]. However, the performance of LLMs can fluctuate heavily depending on the choice of prompts [3,4,5]. While various prompt engineering approaches have been proposed to mitigate this issue, the nontrivial prerequisites of many of these methods, such as training an additional model and/or using an additional component, have been a bottleneck to their real application [6,7,8,9,10,11].

On the other hand, probability-based prompt selection methods do not require any additional parameter updates or additional components and thus provide a promising and easily applicable solution; these methods aim to select, from a set of prompts, the prompt that is expected to be most effective in helping a language model make correct predictions, based solely on the probability distribution of the model [14,5,15,16,17]. However, despite their ease of use, there has been no comprehensive comparative evaluation of existing probability-based prompt selection methods, as each method is proposed in a different setup and evaluated on different datasets, evaluation instances, sets of prompts, and models.

In this paper, we first carefully design a unified evaluation setup to allow a fair comparison between different prompt selection methods. Our unified evaluation reveals that no single method consistently outperforms the others across all datasets, and that all existing probability-based prompt selection methods roughly correspond to a sub-term of the equation of Mutual Information (MI) [14]. We use this discovery to propose several variants of MI that use different combinations of the components of existing methods, and the best combinational variant MI {}_{\textnormal{AGL}} increases the scaled F1 (F1 divided by that of the oracle prompt, showing the effectiveness of the prompt selection method) from 87.79% to 94.98% (MI {}_{\textnormal{AGL}} of Figure 1(a)).

Furthermore, since all probability-based prompt selection methods rely on probabilistic estimates from the model that might be biased, we find the need for a better approximation of the LLM's output probability distribution. Therefore, by drawing a connection between existing model output probability calibration methods [3,4], we propose an enhanced calibration method, Calibration By Marginalization (CBM). When applied to calibrate the output probability of LLMs, CBM significantly improves the prompt selection performance of several methods, increasing the best scaled F1 to 96.85% (MI {}_{\text{A}}^{\text{(PA)}} of Figure 1(a)) and achieving 99.44% of the oracle prompt F1 under the uncalibrated scenario. CBM also shows the most robust answer selection enhancement across multiple datasets compared to existing calibration methods (Figure 1(b)).
